query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled, moderate level of boron microalloying into high-entropy alloys (HEAs) promotes the in situ formation of fine TiB2 precipitates, which refine the microstructure and stabilize the passive film, thereby synergistically reducing both wear and corrosion in harsh, tribocorrosive environments.
generation.material_initial_state: An AlCoCrFeNiMo-based HEA without boron addition, exhibiting coarser grains and a relatively less uniform passive film.
generation.intervention: Controlled addition of a moderate amount of boron to induce in situ precipitation of TiB2 during processing.
generation.conditions: Tribocorrosion tests in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution with a linear reciprocating sliding load (e.g., 5 N, 30-minute duration) at ambient temperature, ensuring both mechanical wear and corrosive exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: Fine, dispersed TiB2 precipitates within the HEA matrix that contribute to grain refinement and enhance the integrity of the passive oxide film.
generation.mechanism: The boron induces the formation of TiB2 particles that act as hard reinforcements, increasing microhardness and reducing wear. Simultaneously, these fine particles promote a more continuous and defect-free passive film, thereby lowering active corrosion sites. In contrast, excessive boron could agglomerate into oversized TiB2, acting as passive film defects.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy without boron, the boron-microalloyed HEA is predicted to exhibit a lower coefficient of friction, reduced wear volume, smaller fluctuations in open-circuit potential, and decreased corrosion current density. The improvements should be evident at optimal boron levels but diminish or reverse if boron is in excess.
generation.baseline: AlCoCrFeNiMo-based HEA prepared without boron microalloying, showing lower microhardness and a less stable passive film under identical tribocorrosion conditions.
generation.boundary: The predicted benefits hold under controlled boron levels and moderate tribocorrosion conditions (ambient temperature, 3.5% NaCl). The hypothesis may fail if boron content is too high (leading to large, deleterious TiB2 particles) or if testing conditions (e.g., high temperatures) promote passive film breakdown beyond the stabilizing capacity of the microstructure.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal boron concentration and its quantitative impact on wear and corrosion parameters remain to be precisely determined; variations in alloy composition and testing environments may affect the degree of enhancement.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA coatings on identical substrates: one set with the controlled boron microalloying (targeting optimal boron levels) and one set without boron. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion testing in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution using a linear reciprocating friction apparatus under a constant load (e.g., 5 N) for a fixed duration (e.g., 30 minutes). Characterize both the microstructure (via SEM/EDS) and passive film integrity (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy).
measurements: Coefficient of friction (COF) over sliding distance
Corrosion current density from polarization measurements
Microstructural assessment of TiB2 particle size and distribution
Passive film continuity and defect density via microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the boron-microalloyed HEA does not show statistically significant improvements (e.g., lower COF, reduced wear rate, more stable OCP, and lower corrosion current density) compared to the non-alloyed baseline under the same tribocorrosion conditions, or if the passive film is shown to be less continuous or more defect-prone, then the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

The tribocorrosion mechanism of the film was analyzed by a linear reciprocating friction machine configured with three electrodes. Si3N4 ceramic grinding balls (Φ 6 mm) were slid for 30 min at a load of 5 N and a frequency of 1 Hz. Prior to formal testing, the sample was immersed in the electrolytic cell with the corrosion solution until the surface potential was stable. The changes in open circuit potential (OCP) and coefficient of friction (COF) were collected in real time throughout the experiment. The wear rate was obtained by the formula w = V/F × S. And the meanings of each physical quantity are as follows: V (mm3) represents wear volume, F (N) represents applied load and S (m) represents sliding distance.

cited_evidence.kind: web:3.4. Tribocorrosion Performance after Annealing in Air Environment
cited_evidence.text: The influence of thermal shock on the tribocorrosion properties of AlCrTiZrMo HEA films is analyzed by monitoring the fluctuation of the OCP and COF of films in the coupled environment of friction and corrosion, as shown in Figure 10. The fluctuation of the OCP and COF of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 400 °C, 600 °C and 800 °C for 1 h in air are monitored in real time. In the preparation stage, the samples were completely immersed in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution for 1 h to obtain a stable surface potential. The duration of the whole experiment is 50 min. During the no-load phase of 0–10 min, both the OCP and COF curves remain stable. During the 10–40 min loading stage, the appearance of the activation region causes the OCP curve to drop sharply, then fluctuate around a constant value. During the 40–50 min no-loading stage, the lack of load causes re-passivation within the wear track, and the OCP curve gradually returns to stability. Therefore, OCP can be used as a mixed potential to monitor the passivation state within the wear track [,,].

cited_evidence.text: From Figure 10, the OCP curves of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed at 400 °C have similar changes with ΔOCP values of 0.453 and 0.461, respectively. During the rapid sliding, the two curves remain stable due to the dynamic balance between activation and passivation within the wear track [,]. Additionally, the two COFs are 0.13 and 0.09, respectively (Table 5). As shown in Figure 11a,b, many adhesions and furrows are found on the abrasion track of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film and the film annealed for 400 °C. The dense microstructure of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film after annealing at 600 °C and the increased H and E improve the resistance to external damage, resulting in a reduction in ΔOCP, COF and wear rate. The ΔOCP, COF and wear rate of the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C are minimized to 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1, respectively, and no obvious wear characteristics appear in the abrasion track, which means that the film is not destroyed. The wear behavior of as-deposited and annealed CuMoTaWV RHEA films on a 304 stainless-steel substrate against an alloy steel counterball was studied to evaluate the effect of annealing on the adhesion. The coefficient of friction versus sliding distance plot of the RHEA film from as-deposited (wear test at RT) and annealed (wear test at RT and 300 °C) films is shown in Figure 11. The wear test of the as-deposited RHEA film showed an average coefficient of friction (COF) of 0.2 up to a sliding distance of 15 m, after which the COF increased to 0.7, suggesting the removal of the film from the substrate. In contrast, the wear behavior of the annealed high-entropy film showed an average COF of 0.25 up to a 30 m sliding distance, followed by a slight increase to 0.3, and remained the same until the end of the test, suggesting an improvement in the film response to wear and its adhesion to the substrate on annealing. The wear behavior at a test temperature of 300 °C showed an average COF of 1.5. The high COF at 300 °C relates to the tribochemical reaction of the RHEA film with the steel counterball, where the formation of oxides on the steel counterball can bias the frictional behavior.

reading.lever: Introduce controlled boron microalloying to form in situ TiB2 for microstructure refinement and passive film stabilization.
reading.why: This approach, demonstrated in related HEA coatings, synergistically enhances both wear and corrosion resistance by optimizing the microstructure and passive film integrity.
